title: Work, Energy and Power
summary: ## Work
Work done by a constant force is W = F · d = Fd cos θ. It is a scalar, measured in joules (1 J = 1 N m).

Work is positive when 0° ≤ θ < 90°, as when lifting a bucket or a monkey climbing up a tree. It is negative when 90° < θ ≤ 180°, as with friction on a sliding body or gravity on a rising ball. It is zero when θ = 90° or d = 0: a coolie walking on level ground with a load, the centripetal force on a body in circular motion, or pushing a wall that does not move. Work is maximum when θ = 0°.
In vector form W = F · d = FₓDₓ + F_yD_y. For F = (5i + 3j) N and d = (3i + 4j) m, W = 15 + 12 = 27 J.
Work equals the area under the force–displacement graph.
## Work done by a variable force (spring)
Hooke's law: F = −kx, where k (in N/m) is the spring constant.

The work done in stretching or compressing a spring by x is W = ∫kx dx = ½kx². This is stored as elastic potential energy, so it grows as x²: stretching from 2 cm to 10 cm multiplies the energy 25 times.
## Energy
Kinetic energy is K = ½mv² = p²/2m. If the speed doubles, K becomes 4 times, an increase of 300%. For equal momentum the lighter body has more KE. For equal KE, p ∝ √m and v ∝ 1/√m.
Gravitational potential energy is U = mgh above a chosen reference level. Elastic potential energy is ½kx².
## Work–energy theorem
The work done by the net force equals the change in kinetic energy: W = K_f − K_i.
Example: a 10 kg body at 4 m/s is pushed by 30 N for 2 s. a = 3 m/s², v = 10 m/s, s = 14 m, so W = 30 × 14 = 420 J = 500 − 80 J.
## Conservative and non-conservative forces

For a conservative force, such as gravity or a spring, the work done is independent of the path and zero over a closed path, so mechanical energy (K + U) is conserved. For a non-conservative force, such as friction or air resistance, the work depends on the path and mechanical energy is lost as heat.

Energy can be converted from one form to another but never created or destroyed. A body thrown up has maximum KE at the point of projection and maximum PE at the top. With air resistance its KE at height h is less than ½mv² − mgh.
## Power
Power is the rate of doing work: P = W/t = Fv. The unit is the watt (1 W = 1 J/s). 1 hp = 746 W, and 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J, a unit of energy.
Example: a crane lifting 100 kg through 10 m in 20 s has P = mgh/t = 100 × 10 × 10/20 = 500 W. A body moving at a steady 5 m/s against 3 N of friction loses Fv = 15 W.
## Collisions
Momentum is conserved in all collisions.
Elastic collision: kinetic energy is also conserved. In one dimension, v₁ = [(m₁ − m₂)u₁ + 2m₂u₂]/(m₁ + m₂) and v₂ = [(m₂ − m₁)u₂ + 2m₁u₁]/(m₁ + m₂).
Perfectly inelastic collision: the bodies stick together and KE is lost as heat, sound and deformation. Common velocity v = m₁u₁/(m₁ + m₂) if m₂ is at rest, and K_f/K_i = m₁/(m₁ + m₂).
mcq: A long spring stretched by 2 cm has potential energy V. If it is stretched by 10 cm, its potential energy will be —

mcq.work:
U = ½kx², so U ∝ x².
x increases 5 times (2 cm → 10 cm), so U = 5² × V = 25V.

mcq: The area under a force–displacement graph equals —
If the speed of a body is doubled, its kinetic energy increases by —

mcq.work: K ∝ v². Doubling v makes K four times, i.e. an increase of 4K − K = 3K = 300%.

mcq: A crane lifts 100 kg through 10 m in 20 s (g = 10 m/s²). Its power is —
Two bodies of different masses have equal momentum. Then —
the lighter body has more kinetic energy
the heavier body has more kinetic energy

mcq.work: K = p²/2m. With p the same, K is larger for the smaller m.

mcq: In which case is work done against the gravity of the earth?
A monkey climbs up a tree
A car moves on a level road
A person tries to lift a heavy load but fails
A person lifts a load in an orbiting satellite
A particle is projected at 60° to the horizontal with kinetic energy E. Its kinetic energy at the highest point is —

mcq.work:
At the top only the horizontal velocity u cos 60° = u/2 remains.
KE = ½m(u/2)² = ¼ × ½mu² = E/4.

mcq: A 2 kg body moves at a constant 5 m/s under a constant 3 N force. The power lost to friction is —

mcq.work:
Constant velocity ⇒ friction = applied force = 3 N.
Power lost = Fv = 3 × 5 = 15 W.

objective: Fill in the blanks: (a) The SI unit of energy is ______. (b) 1 horsepower = ______ watt.
(a) What angle between force and displacement gives maximum work? (b) A light and a heavy body have the same momentum — which has more KE?
State True or False: (a) Work done by a conservative force over a closed path is zero. (b) In an inelastic collision momentum is not conserved.

(a) True.
(b) False — momentum is conserved in all collisions; only KE is lost.

vsa: What are conservative forces? Give one example.

A force is conservative if the work it does is independent of the path and zero over any closed path, so mechanical energy is conserved. Examples: gravitational force, spring force, electrostatic force.
A 100 kg body is lifted 8 m in 10 s. Calculate the power supplied. (g = 9.8 m/s²)
Convert (a) 7460 W into hp and (b) 360 kJ into kWh.
A particle moving with kinetic energy 3.6 J hits a spring of force constant 180 N/m. Find the maximum compression.

All the KE becomes spring energy: ½kx² = 3.6.
x² = 2 × 3.6/180 = 0.04 ⇒ x = 0.2 m.
A ball is thrown vertically up. Where is its (i) kinetic energy and (ii) potential energy maximum?

(i) KE is maximum at the point of projection (and on return), where speed is greatest.
(ii) PE is maximum at the highest point, where it momentarily stops.
Two particles of different masses have equal kinetic energies. Find the ratio of their momenta and velocities.

K = p²/2m ⇒ p = √(2mK), so p₁/p₂ = √(m₁/m₂).
K = ½mv² ⇒ v = √(2K/m), so v₁/v₂ = √(m₂/m₁).
sa: What is meant by positive, negative and zero work? Give an example of each.

W = Fd cos θ.
Positive work (θ < 90°): a person lifting a bucket — force and displacement are both upward.
Negative work (θ > 90°): friction on a sliding body acts opposite to its displacement.
Zero work (θ = 90° or d = 0): a coolie carrying a load on level ground — the upward force is perpendicular to the horizontal motion.

or: State whether the work is positive, negative or zero: (a) friction on a body sliding down an incline; (b) a man lifting a bucket out of a well; (c) a coolie walking on a level platform with a load.

(a) Negative — friction acts up the incline, opposite to the motion.
(b) Positive — the force and the displacement are both upward.
(c) Zero — the force (upward support) is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement.

sa: A force F = (5i + 3j) N moves a particle through d = (3i + 4j) m. Calculate the work done.
A 2 kg body falls freely from 10 m. Using the work–energy principle find (a) its speed at 6 m above the ground, (b) its speed on reaching the ground and (c) the work done by gravity. (g = 10 m/s²)

(a) It has fallen 4 m: ½mv² = mg × 4 ⇒ v = √(2 × 10 × 4) = √80 ≈ 8.9 m/s.
(b) Fallen 10 m: v = √(2 × 10 × 10) = √200 ≈ 14.1 m/s.
(c) W = mgh = 2 × 10 × 10 = 200 J, equal to the gain in KE.
Water falls 51 m at 108 kg per second in a hydroelectric plant. Calculate the work done per second and the power. (g = 9.8 m/s²)

Work per second = mgh = 108 × 9.8 × 51 ≈ 5.4 × 10⁴ J.
Power (ideal) = 5.4 × 10⁴ J/s ≈ 54 kW.
la: State and prove the work–energy theorem. A 10 kg body moving at 4 m/s is acted on by 30 N for 2 s. Find (a) its final speed, (b) the distance covered, (c) the work done and (d) its initial and final KE.

Theorem: the work done by the net force on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy.
Proof (constant force): v² = u² + 2as ⇒ ½mv² − ½mu² = mas = Fs = W.
(a) a = 30/10 = 3 m/s²; v = 4 + 3 × 2 = 10 m/s.
(b) s = ut + ½at² = 8 + 6 = 14 m.
(c) W = Fs = 30 × 14 = 420 J.
(d) Kᵢ = ½ × 10 × 16 = 80 J; K_f = ½ × 10 × 100 = 500 J. Check: 500 − 80 = 420 J = W.

or: Give an example of a variable force and derive the work done by it.

A spring force F = −kx varies with the extension x.
The work done in stretching by a small dx is dW = kx dx. Total work from 0 to x: W = ∫₀ˣ kx dx = ½kx².
This is the area of the triangle under the F–x graph and is stored as elastic potential energy in the spring.

la: A 10 g bullet moving at 100 m/s embeds in a 1 kg wooden block at rest. Find (a) the velocity after collision, (b) the KE before and after, (c) whether the collision is elastic, and (d) the energy lost.

(a) Momentum is conserved: 0.01 × 100 = (0.01 + 1)v ⇒ v = 1/1.01 ≈ 0.99 m/s.
(b) Before: ½ × 0.01 × 100² = 50 J. After: ½ × 1.01 × 0.99² ≈ 0.495 J.
(c) Perfectly inelastic — the bodies stick together and KE is not conserved.
(d) Loss ≈ 50 − 0.5 = 49.5 J, which becomes heat, sound and work in deforming the wood.
Ball A (1 kg) moving at 20 m/s along +x collides elastically with ball B (2 kg) moving at 10 m/s along −x. Find their velocities after the collision.

Momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved.
v_A = [(m_A − m_B)u_A + 2m_Bu_B]/(m_A + m_B) = [(1 − 2) × 20 + 2 × 2 × (−10)]/3 = (−20 − 40)/3 = −20 m/s.
v_B = [(m_B − m_A)u_B + 2m_Au_A]/(m_A + m_B) = [(2 − 1)(−10) + 2 × 1 × 20]/3 = 30/3 = 10 m/s.
So A rebounds at 20 m/s along −x and B moves at 10 m/s along +x.
Check: momentum before = 20 − 20 = 0; after = −20 + 20 = 0.
